short: A month-long rising in 1221 that settled who ruled Japan for the next century.
full:
In the sixth month of 1221 the retired emperor Go-Toba issued a decree branding the Kamakura regent Hōjō Yoshitoki a rebel and summoning the warrior houses of the country to destroy him. He expected the shogunate's vassals to defect. Instead Hōjō Masako reminded the assembled retainers what Minamoto no Yoritomo had given them, and an army said to number nineteen thousand marched west along three roads. The court's forces tried to hold the bridges at Uji and Seta and were broken. Kyoto fell within about a month of the decree.

The settlement was severe. Three retired emperors — Go-Toba, Tsuchimikado and Juntoku — were sent into exile, the reigning Emperor Chūkyō was deposed after seventy-eight days, and some three thousand estates belonging to the defeated were confiscated and handed to Kamakura vassals, extending warrior landholding deep into western Japan. A shogunal deputy, the Rokuhara tandai, was installed in the capital to police the court. The Kamakura shogunate now decided the succession itself.
